artiest/tommy-flanagan.text:
Tommy Flanagan was an American jazz pianist and composer. He was born in Detroit in 1930, the youngest of six children. He began on clarinet, but soon chose piano. Art Tatum, Teddy Wilson and Nat King Cole were his first models, followed by bebop, above all through Bud Powell. In Detroit he played with Kenny Burrell, Pepper Adams and Donald Byrd, among others.

In 1956 he moved to New York. Within a few months he was recording with Miles Davis and on Sonny Rollins's Saxophone Colossus. In 1957 he made his first album of his own in Sweden, Overseas, with the bassist Wilbur Little and the drummer Elvin Jones. In May 1959 he played on John Coltrane's Giant Steps, and in 1960 on Wes Montgomery's The Incredible Jazz Guitar of Wes Montgomery. From 1962 to 1965 and from 1968 to 1978 he was Ella Fitzgerald's pianist, in the last years also her musical director. He was not a vocal accompanist who stayed in the background: during her concerts he often played a trio set of his own.

After leaving Fitzgerald he built a reputation as a leader of piano trios, including with the bassist George Mraz and later Peter Washington. The album The Tommy Flanagan Tokyo Recital from 1975 was his first as a leader since 1960. His playing was known for its elegance and control: he played the melody with respect, yet changed it all the same. At his death in 2001 he was regarded as one of the most admired jazz pianists, also among his colleagues.
artiest/tommy-flanagan.listen: Listen to Giant Steps by John Coltrane and notice Flanagan's piano among the rapidly changing chords. Can you hear where he sounds uncertain?

artiest/tommy-jarrell.text:
Tommy Jarrell was an American fiddler, banjo player and singer from the area around Mount Airy in the Appalachians of North Carolina. He was born in 1901 in Surry County and earned his living in road construction. Until his retirement in 1966 he drove a road grader for the state of North Carolina. Even so, he became an influential musician. In 1982 he received the National Heritage Fellowship from the National Endowment for the Arts, the highest American honour for folk and traditional arts. It was the first year that the award was presented.

His style stands out for an expressive use of syncopation and sliding ornaments, and he could sing well while playing. His strong technique and rough tone continue to inspire young lovers of old-time music, especially for the Round Peak style of clawhammer banjo. His albums include Down to the Cider Mill from 1968, Back Home in the Blue Ridge from 1970 and June Apple from 1972. Les Blank made two documentaries about him, Sprout Wings and Fly and My Old Fiddle. He died in 1985. His first fiddle, which he bought for ten dollars, is now in the possession of the Smithsonian. Every year a festival is held in his honour in Mount Airy.

For the history of popular music Jarrell is important because he was a living link with the music of the Appalachians, which later had an effect on the folk revival and on country and bluegrass. He showed how an old dance music of ordinary people became a source for much later music.
artiest/tommy-jarrell.listen: Listen to Sally Ann and notice the fiddle. Can you hear how Jarrell lets the notes slide and how the bow carries the rhythm?

artiest/tommy-ramone.text:
Tommy Ramone was born Tamás Erdélyi in Budapest in 1949. His parents were Jewish photographers who survived the war because neighbours hid them. In 1957 the family emigrated to the United States and eventually ended up in Forest Hills in Queens, New York. There at school he played guitar in a garage band with John Cummings, the later Johnny Ramone. After school he worked as an assistant at the Record Plant recording studio, on Jimi Hendrix's Band of Gypsys among other things.

When the Ramones came into being, Tommy was meant to be the manager. He had never drummed before, but became the drummer when Joey Ramone became the singer, because Joey could not keep up with the ever faster tempos. From 1974 to 1978 he played on the first three albums, Ramones, Leave Home and Rocket to Russia, and on the live album It's Alive. He was also the co-producer. He wrote I Wanna Be Your Boyfriend and most of Blitzkrieg Bop, for which Dee Dee came up with the title. He himself named the New York Dolls, Lou Reed and Andy Warhol as important influences.

In 1978 he handed over the drumming to Marky Ramone, but he remained involved as manager and producer, including of Road to Ruin and later of Too Tough to Die. He also produced Tim by The Replacements. Later he played in the bluegrass duo Uncle Monk. He died in 2014 at the age of 65, the last survivor of the original line-up.
artiest/tommy-ramone.listen: Listen to Blitzkrieg Bop and notice how little the drums need: a tight, fast rhythm without embellishment. Can you hear that this song comes more from the pen of a drummer than of a guitarist?

artiest/tommy-steele.text:
Tommy Steele, really Thomas Hicks, was born in 1936 in Bermondsey, London, and is regarded as the first British teen idol and rock-and-roll star. He worked as a seaman on a Cunard Line ship and learned to play guitar along the way, with country and calypso as his first repertoire. In the summer of 1956 he met the writer Lionel Bart and the actor Mike Pratt in Soho. Together they formed the loose band The Cavemen. A performance at the 2i's Coffee Bar drew the attention of the publicist John Kennedy, who arranged a contract with Decca within two weeks.

His first single Rock with the Caveman reached number 13 in the British charts in November 1956, and Singing the Blues reached number one in January 1957. His 1957 film The Tommy Steele Story produced the first British number one on the album chart by a British artist, and A Handful of Songs won an Ivor Novello Award in 1958. The press called him Britain's Elvis, although his stage presence was friendlier than Presley's. In 1958 he was injured when fans stormed him at a concert in Dundee, after which he turned mainly to the theatre.

In the 1960s he became an all-round entertainer. He played Kipps in Half a Sixpence, first in the West End and on Broadway, and in 1967 in the film. He also appeared in Singin' in the Rain. He wrote books and made sculpture. In 2020 he was knighted. His importance lies in the fact that he showed that a British boy could achieve stardom in a world that mainly looked to America.
artiest/tommy-steele.listen: Listen to Singing the Blues and notice the light, friendly tone of the singing. Compare this with what you know of Elvis: what is missing here, or simply different?

artiest/ton-koopman.text:
Ton Koopman is a Dutch conductor, organist, harpsichordist and musicologist. He was born in Zwolle in 1944 and studied organ, harpsichord and musicology in Amsterdam. His harpsichord teacher was Gustav Leonhardt. He earned the Prix d'Excellence for both organ and harpsichord and specialised in Baroque music.

In 1979 he founded the Amsterdam Baroque Orchestra, followed in 1992 by the Amsterdam Baroque Choir. Together they now form the Amsterdam Baroque Orchestra & Choir. In 1984 he also founded the Portland Baroque Orchestra. Koopman is one of the leading figures of the historically informed performance movement. That means that he plays on instruments from the composer's time or on exact copies, often with historical tunings, and follows the playing style of the day. He concentrates on Baroque music, above all that of Bach, and draws the line at the death of Mozart in 1791.

His biggest project was the recording of all of Bach's cantatas, which was completed in 2005. When his record company closed its French branch, he bought back the rights and continued the series on his own label Antoine Marchand. He then recorded the complete works of Dieterich Buxtehude, the teacher and predecessor of Bach, which was completed in 2014. Koopman is a professor at the Royal Conservatoire in The Hague and at Leiden University, and in 2003 was made a knight in the Order of the Netherlands Lion.
artiest/ton-koopman.listen: Listen to a Bach cantata in Koopman's performance and notice the sound of the instruments from Bach's time. Can you hear how the organ or the harpsichord supports the singing?

artiest/toni-stern.text:
Toni Stern was an American songwriter and poet, born on 4 November 1944. She died on 17 January 2024, at the age of seventy-nine. She is best known as a lyricist for Carole King, with whom she collaborated in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Stern wrote the words, King composed the music. That is how they worked on It's Too Late, a song about a relationship that is over.

It's Too Late appeared on King's 1971 album Tapestry, one of the best-known albums of the singer-songwriter tradition. What makes Stern's contribution so special is the lyric: a sober, almost calm look back at a love that no longer works, without blame and without drama. In those days few women wrote the lyrics for pop songs that were sung by another woman, and Stern managed to add a personal voice of her own to King's music.

In 2017 Stern published As Close as I Can, a book of her poems. Her name is less often in the foreground than King's, but her work shows how important a lyricist is in a pop song. Anyone who listens to It's Too Late hears two handwritings: that of the composer and that of the writer of the words.
artiest/toni-stern.listen: Listen to It's Too Late by Carole King. Notice how the music stays calm while Toni Stern's lyric describes the end of a relationship almost matter-of-factly.

artiest/tonus-peregrinus.text:
Tonus Peregrinus is a British vocal ensemble devoted to early music and to contemporary sacred music, above all that of its founder and director Antony Pitts. The ensemble was founded in 1990 and made many CDs for the label Naxos. The first, with Arvo Pärt's Passio, won the Cannes Classical Award. For Hyperion two albums appeared with music by Pitts, Seven Letters and Alpha and Omega. The ensemble also sang at the memorial for Alexander Litvinenko.

The titles of the recordings show how wide the repertoire is. Among them are The Mass of Tournai and St Luke Passion (2003), Sacred Music from Notre-Dame Cathedral (2005), Sweet Harmony: Masses and Motets (2005) and Hymns and Songs of the Church (2006). The group also recorded Le Jeu de Robin et de Marion (2006), a medieval musical play, and later Jerusalem-Yerushalayim (2017). In 2012 came Music from the Eton Choirbook, recorded with a new microphone technique developed by the NRK engineer Geoff Miles.

The ensemble is therefore not tied to a single period: it sings early music and new sacred works, including those of its own director. It is best heard on recordings, and the CDs on Naxos and Hyperion form the core of what the group has recorded.
artiest/tonus-peregrinus.listen: Listen to Arvo Pärt's Passio as performed by Tonus Peregrinus and notice how the voices together form a single sound.

artiest/tonus-peregrinus-en-antony-pitts.text:
Tonus Peregrinus is a British vocal ensemble that specialises in early music and in contemporary religious music. Antony Pitts founded it in 1990 and directs it. The ensemble recorded many CDs for Naxos. The first album, Arvo Pärt's Passio, won the Cannes Classical Award. For Hyperion it made two albums with music by Pitts himself, Seven Letters and Alpha and Omega. The album Music from the Eton Choirbook was recorded with a new microphone technique by the NRK engineer Geoff Miles. The ensemble also sang at the memorial for Alexander Litvinenko.

In the course the ensemble appears with Viderunt omnes, a two-part organum by Léonin, from around 1170. Léonin belongs to the composers of Notre-Dame in Paris. Organum is one of the oldest forms of polyphonic music in the West: above a long, sustained Gregorian melody, a second voice sings a freer line. A small group of singers can make this music sound good, because each voice remains audible.

In this way the recording forms a bridge between medieval church music and the centuries that followed. Anyone who wants to hear what the beginning of polyphony sounded like will find a clear rendering here.
artiest/tonus-peregrinus-en-antony-pitts.listen: Listen to Viderunt omnes and notice the long, sustained notes in the lower voice. Can you hear how the upper voice sings a freer line above them?

artiest/tony-allen.text:
Tony Allen was born in Lagos in 1940 and began drumming at eighteen, while working as a technician at a radio station. He listened to juju and highlife, but also to American jazz. He studied the drummers Art Blakey and Max Roach in particular, closely. Through Victor Olaiya's highlife band he came to Fela Kuti in 1964, who invited him to join a jazz-highlife band that was being formed.

From 1969 Allen was the musical director of Africa '70, the band with which Kuti developed a new, militant African sound: the heavy groove of soul, mixed with jazz, highlife and the layered rhythms of the Yoruba. Allen recorded more than thirty albums with Kuti and wrote his own drum parts. He played four rhythms at once, with hands and feet, and that gives Afrobeat its rolling, never-stopping engine. His first solo records were Jealousy in 1975, Progress in 1977 and No Accommodation for Lagos in 1979. After that he left Africa '70 and took many musicians with him.

In 1984 Allen moved to London and later to Paris. His work ran from Afrofunk to dub, electronics and hip-hop. He collaborated with Damon Albarn in The Good, the Bad & the Queen and Rocket Juice & the Moon. Kuti once said that Afrobeat would not have existed without Allen, and Brian Eno called him perhaps the greatest drummer ever. He died in 2020.
artiest/tony-allen.listen: Listen to Jealousy and focus only on the drums: how does Allen sustain a pattern that feels tight and loose at the same time? Try to hear the separate layers of hands and feet.

artiest/tony-iommi.text:
Tony Iommi is an English guitarist who founded Black Sabbath in 1968. He was born in 1948 in Birmingham, the child of Italian immigrants, and went to school with the future singer Ozzy Osbourne. He chose guitar after being inspired by Hank Marvin of The Shadows. On his last day of work at a sheet-metal factory, at the age of seventeen, he lost the tips of two fingers of his right hand, his fretting hand, because he plays left-handed. A colleague let him hear a record by Django Reinhardt, who also played with two fingers. Iommi then made fingertip prostheses out of plastic and kept playing.

The accident shaped his sound. He tuned his guitar lower, used light strings and many power chords, and sought out the tritone interval, the devil's interval, for a heavier and darker sound. On Master of Reality from 1971 he tuned up to three semitones below standard, as in Children of the Grave. The bassist Geezer Butler followed his example. In this way he combined bluesy solos, dark riffs in the minor and a heavily distorted sound. Songs such as Paranoid, War Pigs and The Wizard are regarded as examples of his riffs. Black Sabbath was one of the first groups to use low tunings, a technique that became commonplace in heavy metal.

Iommi played on all of Black Sabbath's records, even when the singers changed: Ronnie James Dio replaced Osbourne in 1979. His first real solo album Iommi appeared in 2000. He is known as the Godfather of Heavy Metal.
artiest/tony-iommi.listen: Listen to Children of the Grave from Master of Reality and notice how low and heavy the guitar sounds. Try to hear how the riff keeps returning.

artiest/tony-mansfield.text:
Tony Mansfield, in full Anthony Charles Mansfield, is an English songwriter, musician and producer. He was born in 1955 in Wimbledon, London, and grew up in Clapham. After school he worked briefly in the art department of Decca Records. In 1977 he founded the synth-pop band New Musik, in which he sang, played guitar and keyboards and wrote most of the songs. The group existed from 1979 to 1982. Its first hit was Straight Lines in 1979, followed by This World of Water, Sanctuary and Living by Numbers in 1980. It made the albums From A to B, Anywhere and Warp.

After the band ended, Mansfield devoted himself entirely to producing. In the 1980s he used the Fairlight CMI, an early sampler and synthesizer, both for preparation and for production. He worked on the debut album by Naked Eyes, Burning Bridges from 1983, with Always Something There to Remind Me. With Captain Sensible he wrote hits such as Glad It's All Over. His first production of Take On Me for a-ha, from the album Hunting High and Low of 1984, was later re-recorded by Alan Tarney, but his influence on the sound of the album was great. He also worked with the B-52's, Mari Wilson and Ana Torroja.

Mansfield's music stands out for its early, inventive use of synthesizers and electronic equipment such as the Korg 700s, the Roland VP-330, the Prophet 5 and the Fairlight. For a pop history without stars he is a good example: a producer who helped define the sound of a decade, even when his name was not in the foreground.
artiest/tony-mansfield.listen: Listen to Take On Me by a-ha. Notice the clear synthesizer lines that carry the melody and how, together with the vocals, they build the song.

artiest/tony-oxley.text:
Tony Oxley was an English drummer in free improvisation who also made electronic music. He was born in 1938 in Sheffield, first taught himself piano and began drumming at seventeen. During his national service he played in the military band of the Black Watch and studied music theory. He then played in a dance orchestra on the Queen Mary, visiting clubs in New York and hearing great jazz musicians.

In 1966 he moved to London, where he became house drummer at Ronnie Scott's Jazz Club. There he accompanied guest musicians such as Joe Henderson, Lee Konitz, Stan Getz, Sonny Rollins and Bill Evans. From 1969 to 1972 he won the Melody Maker readers' poll for drummers every year. In 1969 he played on John McLaughlin's Extrapolation and, with Derek Bailey, Evan Parker and Kenny Wheeler, formed a quintet that released The Baptised Traveller. In 1970 he helped found the label Incus Records, together with Bailey and others, which would release more than fifty albums. He enlarged his drum kit with amplification and electronics.

Later he played with Anthony Braxton and Cecil Taylor, led the Celebration Orchestra and from 1993 formed a quartet with Tomasz Stańko, Bobo Stenson and Anders Jormin. His last albums, Unreleased 1974-2016 and The New World, appeared on Discus. He died at the end of 2023. Oxley showed that a drummer need not only keep a tempo, but can have a voice of his own.
artiest/tony-oxley.listen: Listen to a track from The Baptised Traveller and notice how the drums do not tightly dictate the tempo, but join in with the other instruments. Who leads the conversation?

artiest/tony-sbarbaro.text:
Tony Sbarbaro, also known as Tony Spargo, was an American jazz drummer from New Orleans. He was born in 1897 into an Italian immigrant family and played in local bands early on, including the Frayle Brothers Band and Papa Jack Laine's Reliance Band. His name is above all associated with the Original Dixieland Jazz Band. He was there when that group made its first recordings in 1917, became its leader in 1925 and remained a member until the band stopped in the 1960s. At that point he was the only founder still playing. The group's Darktown Strutters' Ball from 1917, then still written as Original Dixieland Jass Band, was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2006.

Sbarbaro played a drum kit with many individual touches. He used woodblocks, cowbells and Chinese tom-toms, struck the bass drum with the thick end of the stick and even put stuffed toys in the drums to change the sound. A kazoo was also attached to his kit for sound effects. He also wrote music for the group, such as Mourning Blues.

He remained a fixture of Dixieland jazz all his life and later played with Miff Mole, Pee Wee Erwin and Eddie Condon, among others. In the 1960s he gave up music, because rock and roll was displacing Dixieland. He died in 1969 in New York, aged 72.
artiest/tony-sbarbaro.listen: Listen to Darktown Strutters' Ball and notice the drums: among the horns you mainly hear a busy, colourful rhythm with extra sound effects.

artiest/tony-sheridan.text:
Tony Sheridan, in full Anthony Esmond Sheridan McGinnity, was an English rock 'n' roll guitarist who lived in Germany for a large part of his life. He was born in 1940 in Norwich. At seven he played violin, later it became guitar. In 1956 he formed his first skiffle band. He played at the 2i's coffee bar in Soho, appeared in 1958 on the television show Oh Boy! and in England accompanied artists such as Gene Vincent and Conway Twitty. In 1960 he toured with Vincent and Eddie Cochran. Johnny Foster was looking for him for Cliff Richard's band, but at the 2i's found Hank Marvin instead of him.

Because Sheridan was considered unreliable in England, he went to Hamburg in 1960, where until 1963 he played with changing backing bands. There the Beatles met him. In 1961 they stood closer to him and sometimes accompanied him, while he reinforced their performances on guitar. On 22, 23 and 24 June 1961 he recorded a series of songs for Polydor under the direction of Bert Kaempfert, including My Bonnie and The Saints, with the Beatles as accompaniment. The sleeve said The Beat Brothers. In this way he became the only non-Beatle to appear as lead singer on a Beatles recording that reached the charts as a single.

In the mid-1960s Sheridan chose a more blues- and jazz-oriented sound, which disappointed some fans. Later he kept performing in Germany, recorded an album in Los Angeles in 1978 with Elvis Presley's band and released the album Vagabond in 2002. He died in 2013. His name remains linked with the beginnings of the Beatles in Hamburg.
artiest/tony-sheridan.listen: Listen to My Bonnie by Tony Sheridan and The Beat Brothers. Notice how the Scottish folk song begins slowly and then speeds up into a rock 'n' roll number.

artiest/tony-visconti.text:
Tony Visconti was born in 1944 in Brooklyn, New York, into a family of Italian descent. As a teenager he played ukulele, guitar, tuba and double bass, and in the 1960s he worked as a guitarist in nightclubs and small bands. In 1966 he had a modest regional success with his then wife under the name Tony and Siegrid. In 1968 he moved to London, after the producer Denny Cordell had asked him to work on recordings by Georgie Fame. There he grew into one of the most important producers of British pop music.

His first big hit was Ride a White Swan by T. Rex in 1970. With Marc Bolan he made a series of hits, with Electric Warrior in 1971 as the high point. He also produced the first records of Gentle Giant and Osibisa, worked with The Iveys, the later Badfinger, and wrote the string arrangements for Paul McCartney and Wings' Band on the Run. Later he worked with the Moody Blues, the Manic Street Preachers and Angelique Kidjo, among others, for whom he won a Grammy.

His longest collaboration was with David Bowie. From 1968 until Blackstar in 2016 he produced a large part of Bowie's records, including Low and Heroes from 1977. A producer like Visconti is rarely visible, yet he determines the sound: how the drums sound, how the space is built up, which instruments are given the foreground. In the story of pop music behind the Iron Curtain he turns up as the man who assisted Bowie in Berlin on the recordings in which the singer Antonia Maass also took part.
artiest/tony-visconti.listen: Listen to Heroes by David Bowie and notice the drums and the reverberant space around the vocals. Try to hear how the producer makes the sound so big that it seems as if the band is playing in a large hall.

artiest/tony-williams.text: The drummer Tony Williams grew up in Boston and as a boy studied the playing of Max Roach and Art Blakey. At seventeen, in 1963, he became the drummer of Miles Davis's second quintet. His playing was fast and mobile: he often did not spell out the beat, but let the cymbals and the hi-hat move freely around it. In 1969 he founded The Tony Williams Lifetime with the guitarist John McLaughlin and the organist Larry Young, one of the first fusion bands. Emergency! sounded loud and raw like rock music. Later he played acoustic jazz again. He died in 1997 after an operation.
artiest/tony-williams.listen: Listen to the cymbals: a stream of ticks that pushes the band forward.

artiest/toon-hermans.text:
Toon Hermans was born in 1916 in Sittard and grew into one of the most popular cabaret performers in the Netherlands. He began performing in the 1930s and broke through after the war. Together with Wim Sonneveld and Wim Kan he was regarded in the 1950s and 1960s as one of the three greats of Dutch cabaret. He also performed in Flanders, Germany and Austria and in 1968 made an attempt on Broadway.

Hermans did something different from his colleagues. Sonneveld was more intricate and reflective, Kan became increasingly political, but Hermans chose accessible humour about ordinary life. In his one-man shows he told stories from his youth in a small town in Limburg, full of relatives, neighbours, friends and animals. Between the stories came simple, melodious songs about life, love and happiness. Many of those shows were released on record, starting with his one-man show from 1958. He also wrote poems.

His best-known song is Vierentwintig rozen, which returned in many shows. It consists of a long accumulation of separate images, different each time, that ends with the roses. His 1967 show is said to have been seen on television by six million people, half of the Netherlands. Critics of later decades found him too innocent, but the audience kept coming. After the death of his wife in 1990 he made a performance with songs only, in a blend of simple jazz and chanson. In the Nederpop chapter of School of Rock he belongs among the big names from the theatre, where the Dutch-language song long came from.
artiest/toon-hermans.listen: Listen to Vierentwintig rozen in one of his recordings. Notice how the song lists a long row of separate images and how the tension builds towards the roses.

artiest/toontje-lager.text:
Toontje Lager is a Dutch-language pop group from Wageningen. The band began in 1977 under the shocking name Maandverband (Dutch for sanitary towel), founded by Bert Vermaas, Frits Raijmakers and Bert Hermelink. The first performance was in café Troost in Wageningen, with ten punk and rock songs in Dutch, which they played twice to fill the evening. In 1978 the group carried on in a new line-up as Toontje Lager. With the singer Vermaas the first album appeared in 1980. The song Kontaktrock was on the compilation Uitholling overdwars, which gave the revival of Dutch-language pop a considerable push.

After Vermaas left, Erik Mesie became the singer. The keyboardist Bert Hermelink wrote by far the most songs. In the early 1980s the hits came: Stiekem gedanst, Zoveel te doen and Net als in de film. The albums Er op of er onder (1982) and Stiekem dansen (1983) were awarded gold. Listeners of the radio station Hilversum 3 chose In gedachten, the B-side of Ben jij ook zo bang, as B-side of the year. A passage from Zoveel te doen was for years the theme tune of the motoring programme De heilige koe. In 1983 the group received the Zilveren Harp, a Dutch music award.

Toontje Lager belonged to the wave of bands who made pop music in Dutch around 1980, together with Doe Maar, Het Goede Doel and the Frank Boeijen Groep, among others. In 1985 the group split up. Hermelink became a cabaret performer. Since 2019 Mesie has been performing again with a new line-up of Toontje Lager.
artiest/toontje-lager.listen: Listen to Stiekem gedanst. Notice how the keyboards and Erik Mesie's vocals together carry the melody, and how naturally Dutch lyrics sound here in a pop song from the early 1980s.

artiest/toots-en-the-maytals.text:
Toots & The Maytals is a group from Jamaica built around the singer Frederick Toots Hibbert. He was born in 1942 in May Pen, sang gospel in a church choir as a child and moved to Kingston in the late 1950s. There in 1962 he formed the vocal trio The Maytals with Henry Raleigh Gordon and Nathaniel Jerry Mathias. They made their first recordings at Studio One with the producer Coxsone Dodd, with The Skatalites as backing band. With their gospel-style close harmony singing they were then more popular than The Wailers.

In 1966 they won the first Jamaican song festival around independence with Bam Bam. Hibbert then spent eighteen months in prison; he wrote 54-46 That's My Number about that time. With the producer Leslie Kong came a series of hits, including Do the Reggay (1968), the first song with the word reggae in it. Pressure Drop, Sweet and Dandy and Monkey Man also became well known. In the 1970s the group signed with Chris Blackwell's Island Records, appeared in the film The Harder They Come and made Funky Kingston (1973) and Reggae Got Soul (1976). Hibbert died in 2020.

The Maytals helped take the music of Jamaica from ska through rocksteady to reggae, and brought it to a worldwide audience. Hibbert's raw, fiery voice was often compared with that of Otis Redding. During the ska revival around 1979 The Specials recorded Monkey Man and The Clash covered Pressure Drop. The Oxford English Dictionary cites the group in the origin of the word reggae.
artiest/toots-en-the-maytals.listen: Listen to Do the Reggay and notice the rhythm: slower than ska, with the emphasis on the offbeat and a prominent bass line. Hear how Toots announces the new dance with a voice still full of gospel.

artiest/toots-hibbert.text:
Toots Hibbert was a Jamaican singer and songwriter, the lead singer of Toots and the Maytals. He was born in 1942 in May Pen, the youngest child of strict Adventist preachers. He grew up with gospel in the church choir. At the age of eleven he was an orphan and went to live with his brother in Trenchtown, Kingston. At a barber's he met Raleigh Gordon and Jerry Matthias, with whom he formed the Maytals in 1961. His great examples were Otis Redding, Ray Charles, Wilson Pickett and James Brown.

In the mid-1960s the Maytals were one of the most popular vocal groups in Jamaica. Hibbert wrote Bam Bam, Sweet and Dandy and Pomps & Pride, which all won the national song competition. In 1966 he was locked up for 18 months for possession of marijuana, which inspired 54-46 That's My Number. His song Do the Reggay from 1968 is regarded as the source of the word reggae. Pressure Drop and the album Funky Kingston on Island Records followed. In the film The Harder They Come the group plays Sweet and Dandy, and Pressure Drop is on the soundtrack.

Hibbert kept performing for six decades. The album Live from 1980 was released within a day of being recorded, which got into the Guinness Book of World Records. In 2005 True Love won a Grammy for Best Reggae Album. He died in 2020. His voice, shaped by gospel and soul, gave reggae a warmth of its own.
artiest/toots-hibbert.listen: Listen to Pressure Drop and notice Hibbert's singing, which sounds raw and soulful. Can you hear gospel in the way he sings?

artiest/toots-thielemans.text: Jean-Baptiste 'Toots' Thielemans from Brussels began on the accordion and learned to play guitar during the war, inspired by Django Reinhardt. He also played harmonica, and it was on that instrument that he became world-famous. In 1952 he moved to the United States, where he played with George Shearing. His melody Bluesette (1962), which he played whistling along with the guitar, became a hit and a standard. His harmonica can be heard in films such as Midnight Cowboy and in the Sesame Street theme. He played with Quincy Jones, Bill Evans and Jaco Pastorius. He was made a baron by the Belgian king and died in 2016.
artiest/toots-thielemans.listen: Listen to the harmonica: singing and melancholy, like a human voice.

artiest/toru-takemitsu.text: Tōru Takemitsu (1930–1996) was almost entirely self-taught and began in the artists' group Jikken Kōbō, where he experimented with tape and electronics. He wrote music for nearly a hundred films. In them he worked like a sound designer: in Seppuku (1962) the biwa sounds alongside electronically processed sounds, in Suna no onna (1964) strings are treated so that they resemble sand and wind, and in Kaidan (1964) he used sounds such as breaking wood. For Kurosawa's Ran (1985), by contrast, he wrote a large orchestral work reminiscent of Mahler. He allowed a great deal of silence and used music sparingly, which made his influence on later film composers great.
artiest/toru-takemitsu.listen: Listen to the tone colour rather than the melody: long, floating chords, silence as part of the music and processed instrumental sounds.

artiest/toshiko-akiyoshi.text: Toshiko Akiyoshi was born in 1929 in Manchuria, where her Japanese family lived. After the war the family returned to Japan. She played piano in dance clubs for American soldiers and learned bebop from records by Bud Powell. When the pianist Oscar Peterson heard her in Tokyo, the producer Norman Granz had her make a record in 1953. In 1956 she went to Berklee in Boston as the first Japanese student. With her husband, the saxophonist Lew Tabackin, she started a big band in Los Angeles in 1973. For it she wrote pieces with Japanese elements, such as Kogun (1974), in which drums and voices from Noh theatre can be heard.
artiest/toshiko-akiyoshi.listen: Listen to how Japanese drums and voices combine with the sound of an American big band.

artiest/toto.text:
Toto is an American rock band from Los Angeles, founded in 1977 by the keyboardist David Paich and the drummer Jeff Porcaro. They knew each other from secondary school and were sought-after session musicians: they played on records by Steely Dan, Sonny & Cher and Boz Scaggs, among others, for whom Paich wrote a large part of Silk Degrees. The bassist David Hungate, the guitarist Steve Lukather, the keyboardist Steve Porcaro and the singer Bobby Kimball completed the band. The name was on their demo tapes; Hungate pointed out that the Latin in toto means all-embracing, and that suited musicians who were at home in every style.

The debut album Toto (1978) produced the hit Hold the Line. After Hydra (1979) and Turn Back (1981) came the great success with Toto IV (1982). Africa was number one in America in February 1983, Rosanna became a big hit, and the album won six Grammys. At the same time Steve Porcaro co-wrote Human Nature for Michael Jackson's Thriller, and Jeff Porcaro and Lukather played on that album, including on Beat It. After that the band often changed singers. Jeff Porcaro died in 1992; the band carried on until Old Is New (2018).

Toto blended pop, rock, soul, funk, jazz and prog rock into a tight, polished sound. Critics often found the music too slick, but the musicians were regarded as top-class professionals. The fact that the band both scored hits of its own and played on other people's records shows how session musicians in Los Angeles helped shape the pop music of the 1970s and 1980s.
artiest/toto.listen: Listen to Africa and notice the rhythm: the drums and percussion lay a rolling, slightly displaced pattern beneath the song. Hear how the synthesizers and the multi-part vocals in the chorus are stacked on top of it.

artiest/toumani-diabate.text: Toumani Diabaté came from a griot family that has played the kora for many generations, the West African harp with 21 strings. His father Sidiki made the first album devoted entirely to the kora in 1970. In 1988 Toumani recorded his solo album Kaira in London in a single afternoon, on which he plays bass, melody and improvisation at once. With Ali Farka Touré he won a Grammy for In the Heart of the Moon (2005).
artiest/toumani-diabate.listen: Listen to Jarabi and follow the three layers: a low bass line, a repeated pattern in the middle and fast runs above, all played by one player.

artiest/tpok-jazz.text:
TPOK Jazz, in full Tout Puissant Orchestre Kinois de Jazz, was a Congolese rumba band, founded in 1956 in Léopoldville, present-day Kinshasa, then still in the Belgian Congo. The original name was OK Jazz, after the OK Bar where the musicians played. The first members included Vicky Longomba, Jean Serge Essous and François Luambo Makiadi, better known as Franco. In the early years they shared the leadership. In the early 1960s Longomba and Essous left, and Franco became the leader. The name changed to TPOK Jazz and the number of musicians grew to more than twenty.

Franco's music appealed because it was about the daily lives of ordinary people. He was also one of the first Congolese musicians to use electric guitars, amplifiers and bass guitars, which meant the sound quality was higher than elsewhere in Africa. The guitarist Mose Fan Fan brought the danceable sebene style. In the 1970s the orchestra grew into one of the two giants of Congolese popular music, alongside Grand Kalle & l'African Jazz. In 1978 Franco spent two months in prison over the songs Helene and Jacky, which were considered indecent. The 1980s were the peak, with an average of four albums a year and, in 1983, the first tour of the United States. The song Attention Na Sida from 1987 warned against AIDS.

After Franco's death in 1989 Simaro Lutumba took over the leadership. In 1993 a quarrel arose with Franco's family over income and instruments, after which most of the musicians under Lutumba formed the group Bana OK. A restart in 1996 was inactive again by 2004.
artiest/tpok-jazz.listen: Listen to Attention Na Sida and notice how the singing in French lies over heavy African drums and many guitars. How does the music make the message stronger?

artiest/tracy-chapman.text:
Tracy Chapman is an American singer-songwriter, born in 1964 in Cleveland. Her mother bought a ukulele when she was three, and at eight she was already writing songs on guitar. Through a programme for gifted pupils she went to a boarding school in Connecticut, after which she studied anthropology at Tufts University. There she played on the street in Harvard Square and on subway platforms. A fellow student brought a demo with Talkin' 'bout a Revolution to the attention of a publisher, and in 1987 she signed with Elektra Records.

Her self-titled debut album from 1988 was a great success. A decisive role was played by her performance at the Nelson Mandela 70th Birthday Tribute at Wembley Stadium, where she stepped in at the last moment for Stevie Wonder. After that Fast Car rose quickly in the American charts. The album won three Grammys, including that for Best New Artist. Later came Crossroads (1989), Matters of the Heart (1992) and New Beginning (1995), with the hit Give Me One Reason. Telling Stories, Let It Rain, Where You Live and Our Bright Future (2008) followed.

Her music is sober: an acoustic guitar, a warm, dark voice and lyrics about poverty, inequality and politics. In 2023 Luke Combs had a country hit with his cover of Fast Car, which made Chapman the first Black artist to win a country award for Song of the Year with a composition of her own.
artiest/tracy-chapman.listen: Listen to Fast Car and notice how little there is beneath the voice: mainly guitar. What story do the lyrics tell, and how strong is the melody without drums?

artiest/travis-scott.text:
Travis Scott is an American rapper, singer and producer, born in 1991 as Jacques Bermon Webster II in Houston. His stage name combines the name of his uncle Travis with the first name of his example Kid Cudi. He dropped out of his studies in San Antonio to focus on music, moved to New York and in 2012 signed with Epic Records, with a publishing deal besides at Kanye West's GOOD Music as a producer.

His first mixtapes were Owl Pharaoh (2013) and Days Before Rodeo (2014). The debut album Rodeo appeared in 2015, followed by Birds in the Trap Sing McKnight (2016) and Astroworld (2018). From that last album, Sicko Mode, with Drake, became his first number one on the American Hot 100. Utopia (2023) and the short film Circus Maximus followed. In 2017 he founded the label Cactus Jack Records, which signed artists such as Don Toliver.

His sound blends trap with psychedelic, distorted vocals and many studio effects, with Kanye West and Kid Cudi as influences. He is known for his energetic live performances and for collaborations with fashion brands. At the same time his name is linked with a tragedy: at his Astroworld Festival in Houston in November 2021 a dangerous crowd crush occurred, in which ten people died. This led to much discussion about safety at concerts.
artiest/travis-scott.listen: Listen to Sicko Mode and notice how the song changes in mood, tempo and beat halfway through. How many separate sections can you hear?

artiest/trent-reznor.text:
Trent Reznor was born in 1965 in New Castle, Pennsylvania, and grew up in rural Mercer. He learned piano as a child and at school played tenor saxophone and tuba in the jazz band and the marching band. In 1982 he began in synth-pop bands such as The Innocent, Slam Bamboo and Exotic Birds. In 1988 he founded Nine Inch Nails, of which he was the only official member until 2016. He writes the songs, sings and plays the instruments himself.

The first album Pretty Hate Machine appeared in 1989 and remained popular mainly with an underground audience. The Downward Spiral from 1994 and The Fragile from 1999 brought broad praise from critics. The music combines the coldness of synthesizers and drum machines with the violence of rock, and is called industrial rock. Reznor also worked on records by Marilyn Manson, Saul Williams and Halsey and in 2009 formed the group How to Destroy Angels with his wife and regular collaborators.

Since 2010 he has made film music together with Atticus Ross, mainly for directors such as David Fincher and Luca Guadagnino. For The Social Network and Soul they won an Academy Award for Best Original Score. They also wrote the music for Watchmen and the documentary The Vietnam War. This makes Reznor a rare example of a pop musician who grew into a film composer. In the 1980s chapter of School of Rock he fits as someone who brought synthesizers and aggressive guitars together, as in Head Like a Hole from 1989.
artiest/trent-reznor.listen: Listen to Head Like a Hole by Nine Inch Nails. Notice how the electronic rhythms and the guitars together form a single hard, tight sound.

artiest/trent-reznor-en-atticus-ross.text: Trent Reznor is the founder of the industrial rock band Nine Inch Nails. Atticus Ross is a British producer who has worked with him since 2005. Together they wrote the music for David Fincher's The Social Network (2010). That score, with a simple piano above gritty electronic sounds, won an Oscar. For Fincher they then did The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo (2011) and Gone Girl (2014), among others. They work from the studio: they distort sounds, allow noise in and build up layers into restless soundscapes. For Pixar's Soul (2020) they won a second Oscar, together with Jon Batiste. For Challengers (2024) they made rousing techno music.
artiest/trent-reznor-en-atticus-ross.listen: Notice the contrast between a vulnerable piano melody and the distorted, hissing electronic layers beneath it.

artiest/trevor-horn.text:
Trevor Horn was born in 1949 in Hetton-le-Hole in the north-east of England. His father was a big band musician and taught him the first principles of the double bass. Horn taught himself to play bass guitar and to read music and worked as a session musician in London in the 1970s. He built his own studio and made singles for other artists. In 1979 he had a hit as a member of the Buggles with Video Killed the Radio Star. In 1980 he became the singer of Yes for the album Drama.

From 1981 he worked full-time as a producer. He made records with Dollar, ABC, Malcolm McLaren, Grace Jones, Frankie Goes to Hollywood and the Pet Shop Boys. In 1983 he and his wife Jill Sinclair bought the Sarm West Studios in London, and with the journalist Paul Morley he founded the label ZTT. He was also a co-founder of Art of Noise. Later he produced Seal, t.A.T.u. and Mike Oldfield's Tubular Bells II. He received three Brit Awards as best British producer and a Grammy for Seal's Kiss from a Rose.

Horn is known for big, layered productions in which electronics, studio technique and orchestral effects come together. He has therefore been called the man who invented the 1980s. In School of Rock he returns with ABC, where on The Look of Love from 1982 he put strings and orchestral stabs beneath the pop song and so introduced a new sound.
artiest/trevor-horn.listen: Listen to The Look of Love by ABC. Notice the strings and the short orchestral stabs that make the song dramatic, and ask yourself how the song would sound without that layer.

artiest/trevor-jones.text: Trevor Jones was born in 1949 in Cape Town. With a scholarship he went to the Royal Academy of Music in London in 1967. Later he earned a master's in film and media music at the University of York and attended the National Film and Television School. He worked mainly in Britain. For Jim Henson he wrote The Dark Crystal (1982) and Labyrinth (1986); in Labyrinth his score stands alongside songs by David Bowie. He became best known for The Last of the Mohicans (1992), which he wrote together with Randy Edelman. He also made Excalibur (1981), Mississippi Burning (1988), Brassed Off (1996) and Notting Hill (1999), among others. In 1999 he became the first head of the music department at the National Film and Television School.
artiest/trevor-jones.listen: In The Last of the Mohicans, listen to how a tight, repeated string rhythm builds the tension beneath the broad main theme.

artiest/trevor-pinnock.text:
Trevor Pinnock is a British harpsichordist and conductor, born in 1946 in Canterbury. As a boy he sang in the choir of Canterbury Cathedral, became a church organist and began playing harpsichord at fifteen. At the Royal College of Music he studied organ and harpsichord. One model was Gustav Leonhardt, although he did not study with him. In 1966 he made his London debut with the Galliard Harpsichord Trio, which at that time still played Baroque music on modern instruments.

In November 1972 that trio became The English Concert, an orchestra that plays Baroque and Classical music on period instruments. Pinnock felt that performances on modern instruments had reached an endpoint and wanted to embark on a voyage of discovery. He was one of the pioneers of the historically informed performance movement. In 1975 he played harpsichord in the first-ever performance of Rameau's last opera, Les Boréades. For more than thirty years he led the orchestra, usually from the harpsichord or organ, until he handed over the direction to the violinist Andrew Manze in 2003. He made many recordings with the group, including works by Bach and Handel.

In addition he founded The Classical Band in New York in 1989 and from 1991 to 1996 was music director of the National Arts Centre Orchestra in Ottawa. As a guest conductor he appeared before the Berliner Philharmoniker and the Wiener Philharmoniker, among others. His recording of Bach's Brandenburg Concertos with the European Brandenburg Ensemble won a Gramophone Award. Pinnock showed how lively Baroque music sounds when it comes from the instruments of its own time.
artiest/trevor-pinnock.listen: Listen to a Brandenburg Concerto by Bach in Pinnock's performance and notice the sound of the harpsichord among the strings. How does that differ from a modern symphony orchestra?

artiest/tricky.text:
Tricky, born Adrian Thaws in 1968 in the Knowle West district of Bristol, is one of the founders of trip hop. As a boy he hung around the sound system The Wild Bunch, from which Massive Attack emerged. There he was given the nickname Tricky Kid. On Blue Lines (1991), Massive Attack's debut, he can be heard as a rapper.

His first solo album, Maxinquaye (1995), is named after his late mother, Maxine Quaye. He recorded it largely in a home studio in Kilburn, with Mark Saunders as co-producer. Most of the vocals come from Martina Topley-Bird. Her clear voice stands beside his whispered, hoarse raps. Tricky piled up samples, slow beats and noise into a stifling whole. The album reached number three in the British album chart and was nominated for the Mercury Prize, which went to Portishead's Dummy. In the critics' year-end poll of NME, Maxinquaye was the best record of 1995.

After that his work became darker still, with Pre-Millennium Tension (1996) and the project Nearly God from the same year. Where the softer trip hop ended up in lounges and on chill-out compilations, Tricky stayed with raw, restless sounds. The New York Times called Maxinquaye in 1996 the first album-length masterpiece in trip hop. The album is cited as an influence on electronica, underground hip-hop and British hip-hop. Tricky kept making records and in 2016 was back on stage with Massive Attack.
artiest/tricky.listen: Hell Is Round the Corner runs on a slowed-down loop from Isaac Hayes's Ike's Rap II (1971). Portishead used the same loop in Glory Box, reportedly by coincidence. Put them side by side and hear how one sample carries two very different songs.

artiest/tricky-sam-nanton.text:
Joe Nanton, known as Tricky Sam, was an American trombonist in Duke Ellington's orchestra. He was born in 1904 in New York to immigrants from the British West Indies and first played in Washington, D.C., including in the bands of Cliff Jackson and Elmer Snowden. In 1926 he reluctantly took the place of his friend Charlie Irvis with Ellington, and stayed there until his early death in 1946. Together with Lawrence Brown he formed the backbone of the trombone section.

Nanton was a pioneer of the plunger, the rubber mute that you hold in front of the bell of the horn. In 1921 he heard Johnny Dunn do it on the trumpet and realised that it could also be done on trombone. Together with the trumpeter Bubber Miley he created the typical wah-wah sound. Their growling, almost speaking sounds formed the core of the band's early jungle sound, which arose in the late 1920s at the Cotton Club in Harlem. Nanton used a straight trumpet mute in the bell, a large plunger outside it and meanwhile shaped vowels with his mouth, so that the trombone seemed to talk. He kept the details secret until his death. He got his nickname from the alto saxophonist Otto Hardwick.

Nanton can be heard on East St. Louis Toodle-oo, Black and Tan Fantasy and The Mooche, among others. After Miley left in 1929 he taught Cootie Williams the growling techniques. Many brass players of the swing era adopted his sound. He died in 1946 of a stroke during a tour.
artiest/tricky-sam-nanton.listen: Listen to Black and Tan Fantasy and notice the trombone that almost seems to have a voice. Can you hear the wah-wah, the opening and closing of the plunger?

artiest/tricky-stewart.text:
Tricky Stewart is an American producer, songwriter, music publisher and record executive, born in 1974 in Markham, Illinois. He grew up in a musical family, played guitar and keyboards at twelve and was already writing songs. His older brother, the producer Laney Stewart, put him in touch with the mentor Louis Silas, as a result of which, even before graduating, he supplied songs to Aaron Hall, IMx and Chanté Moore, among others. In 1995, with the support of L.A. Reid, he founded the company RedZone Entertainment, and the studio Triangle Sound, in Atlanta.

His first big success came in 1999 with Who Dat by JT Money. In 2000 he wrote and produced Case of the Ex for Mýa, and then was executive producer of Blu Cantrell's debut album So Blu. He also made Uh Huh for B2K and wrote and produced for Britney Spears, among others, Me Against the Music and Outrageous on In the Zone (2003). He often works with the singer and writer The-Dream. Together they made Umbrella for Rihanna in 2007, Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It) for Beyoncé in 2008 and songs for Mariah Carey and Justin Bieber, such as One Time and Baby.

Stewart has won five Grammys and also signed the singer Frank Ocean to RedZone for his breakthrough. His work shows how in the 2000s the pop sound was shaped by producers behind the scenes: tight rhythms, simple, catchy choruses and R&B singing.
artiest/tricky-stewart.listen: Listen to Umbrella by Rihanna and notice the drum machine and the repetition of the chorus. What makes this chorus so easy to remember?

artiest/trio.text:
Trio was a German group formed in 1979 in Großenkneten. The line-up consisted of Stephan Remmler on vocals and keyboards, Gert Krawinkel, nicknamed Kralle, on guitar and Peter Behrens on drums. At first the band was called Zam. The debut album Trio appeared in 1981, produced by Klaus Voormann, the man who also played bass on a few tracks.

The greatest success was Da Da Da, released in 1982. The song reached number two in Germany and became a hit in thirty countries. Bye Bye followed in 1983 and the film soundtrack Whats the Password in 1985, for the flop Drei gegen Drei. In 1986 the group fell apart, after Behrens quarrelled with the others over money.

Trio belonged to the Neue Deutsche Welle, but preferred to call itself Neue Deutsche Fröhlichkeit. The principle was to leave out everything that was not necessary. The songs often had only three chords and consisted of drums, guitar, vocals and at most one or two other instruments. On stage Remmler played simple rhythms and melodies on a small Casio keyboard. In this way Trio showed that a hit does not have to be polished: the bare, almost childlike approach became an example for later electropop and minimalist new wave.
artiest/trio.listen: Listen to Da Da Da and count how many instruments you hear. Notice how little is needed to make the song work.

artiest/trio-matamoros.text:
The Trío Matamoros was a Cuban trova group from Santiago de Cuba. Miguel Matamoros and Rafael Cueto played guitar, Siro Rodríguez played maracas and claves, and all three sang and composed. They began in 1925 as Trio Oriental and in 1928 changed their name to Trio Matamoros, because a group with the first name already existed. The three stayed together for thirty-five years. In May 1961 they announced their farewell, after a last concert in New York the year before.

The group played boleros and son, toured Latin America and Europe and recorded in New York. Miguel Matamoros wrote much of the repertoire and was one of the most prolific composers of Cuban son. His first hit was El que siembra su maíz. Lágrimas negras and Son de la Loma, among others, followed. In 1934 they recorded a song about the disaster of the ship Morro Castle. For a trip to Mexico Matamoros expanded the trio into a conjunto, with the young Beny Moré as singer from 1945 to 1947.

The group was praised for its harmony singing and the quality of its lyrics. It is regarded as important in the rise of son, which later became the basis for salsa and other Caribbean dance music.
artiest/trio-matamoros.listen: Listen to Son de la Loma and notice how the voices sing together and how the guitars, maracas and claves set down a light, danceable rhythm.

artiest/tristan-honsinger.text:
Tristan Honsinger was an American cellist, active in free jazz and free improvisation. He was born in 1949 in Burlington, Vermont. His mother gave him and his brother and sister music lessons at an early age, in the hope of forming a chamber orchestra, and at twelve he was giving concerts almost weekly. He studied classical cello at the New England Conservatory in Boston and in 1969 moved to Montreal to avoid the draft. There he became interested in improvised music.

In 1974 he moved to Europe, where he worked out of Amsterdam. He played in Misha Mengelberg and Han Bennink's Instant Composers Pool and worked with the guitarist Derek Bailey. In the late 1970s he spent some time in Italy, where he worked with a theatre group and founded a band of his own, This, That, and the Other. His best-known collaboration was with the pianist Cecil Taylor, from the end of the 1980s. He also played with the British post-punk band The Pop Group in 1979 and with the Dutch group The Ex. His albums include Double Indemnity and Imitation of Life, both from the early years of Y Records.

Honsinger was known for his almost comical body language on stage. His compositions were as simple as a child's drawing or a Winnie-the-Pooh story, but with deeper meaning. He often wrote them as stories, so that musicians and audience had something to hold on to. He died in 2023 in Trieste, aged 73.
artiest/tristan-honsinger.listen: Listen to a recording by Honsinger and notice how the cello does not only sing, but also scratches, jumps and talks. Can you hear a small story in it?
